item.title: 🔴 Live: Pope Leo celebrates Mass before hundreds of thousands at Concord in central Paris
item.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he doesn't believe President Trump is "really dug in" against guardrails for AI , despite Trump's public campaign against restricting the technology. Why it matters: Thune told Axios he spoke privately with Trump as the AI issue was getting "pretty hot" a few weeks ago and believes some of Trump's strong pushback is against public "paranoia and noise around the subject." "I don't think it's an issue that he's really dug in on," Thune told Axios. Thune reads Trump's position as a preference for companies coming up with ways to secure their systems, rather than Congress or the administration. That approach relies more on experts to provide guidance. Trump has called recent fears around AI safety a "hoax." item.title: Xi wraps up US visit with trip to National Archives
item.description:
Chinese leader Xi Jinping departed Washington this afternoon after a three-day trip that led to no significant breakthroughs on the two country’s disagreements, including on AI, Taiwan and Iran. Xi broached Taiwan to Trump, per a readout from Beijing, and Trump asked Xi to stop supporting Iran , US Ambassador to Beijing David Perdue said . Officials also discussed extending their trade truce until January and staying in touch about AI, Treasury Department Scott Bessent said earlier this week. But there were no major announcements with the countries still at odds on most fronts, including its growing nuclear arsenal. That could change later this year, when Xi said he would see Trump at the APEC summit in China and the G20 summit in the US. Xi also invited Trump back to China in the spring. item.title: Lula says Trump wants to ‘colonise’ and capture Brazil’s resources by meddling in election
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping landed at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington on Wednesday and was met personally on the tarmac by President Donald Trump. The agenda included an elaborate Rose Garden military review and official state dinner in the White House's East Room. Most of that chichi was just foreplay before Thursday's negotiations to extend the one-year trade war truce between the nations that's set to run out in November. It's quite the welcome for a leader of a country the administration calls America's chief adversary. Then again, it's no easy thing to follow the details of Trump's trade policy. His first term was different. Trump's Section 301 tariffs and most of the other tariffs starting in 2018 were aimed almost exclusively at China. item.title: France: Pope says 'authentic secularity' does not exclude religion
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV said on a visit to France on Friday that "authentic secularity" should not exclude religion, in a country where law has for more than a century separated church and state. "An authentic secularity, then, consists not in excluding religion from the public sphere or from education, but in striving to ensure that the state and religious institutions maintain dialogue and join forces in the service of the common good," he said.

Sources: BBC News, France 24

item.title: Pochettino regrets limited role in Balogun red card decision at World Cup
item.description:
US striker had red card ban suspended for Belgium game Trump said he called Infantino asking for review Coach says ‘energy of everything’ changed in moment US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino has said he regrets not being “more involved” in the situation surrounding US forward Folarin Balogun at this summer’s World Cup. Balogun was given a red card after a challenge against Bosnia and Herzegovina defender Tarik Muharemovic, which by rule is accompanied with a one-game suspension. Balogun’s ban for the next game against Belgium was suspended after the US Soccer Federation and Donald Trump lobbied Fifa , with Trump saying that he personally placed a call to Fifa president Gianni Infantino to ask the ruling be reviewed. Infantino maintains that the decision to reinstate Balogun was made independently by Fifa’s disciplinary committee. Continue reading...

Sources: Al Jazeera English, The Guardian

item.title: Manchester City found guilty? What we know; what could the punishment be?
item.description:
Remember when the Premier League charged Manchester City with over 100 instances of financial maneuvering which ran afoul of league rules? It's possible you've forgotten all about that, since the league's investigation began all the way back in 2019, and the charges were announced in 2023. The long timeline here is owed to City's continued refusal to cooperate with the Premier League and the efforts of their expensive legal teams. But time moves forward nonetheless, and so at long last we hare here, with The Athletic's David Ornstein reporting that City has been found guilty of almost every charge it faced. Since it has been three years since the charges were first announced, a refresher is in order.
